profiles.meeting_scenario: A university-based organizational creativity researcher and a global learning-and-development strategist at a manufacturing firm are holding a brainstorming meeting to shape a joint practitioner-research brief titled "What Do We Really Know About CPS Training at Work?" The brief will be used both for an internal innovation council discussion and as the basis for a conference proposal on Creative Problem Solving (CPS) in organizational settings. Their agenda is to generate promising framing angles, decide what kinds of evidence and examples feel relevant, and sketch 2-3 candidate sections for the brief. The expected outcome is a shared shortlist of ideas for how to position the review and what kinds of workplace cases to highlight, without yet making formal methodological decisions.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Creativity research, training evaluation, evidence synthesis, workplace learning transfer
members.background: Lena studies how structured creativity methods affect employee behavior and has published reviews on applied innovation training; she often collaborates with companies but is trained to frame claims conservatively around research evidence.
members.private_state: She wants the brief to be credible to academics and not look like a promotional piece for CPS vendors; she is especially concerned about overstating workplace impact when evidence comes from short-term or quasi-real business exercises.
hidden_assumptions: When people say CPS was used on "workplace issues," the problems should be real, current organizational challenges owned by people in those jobs, not classroom-simulated business cases.
"Effectiveness" implies evidence of change beyond the training room, ideally some delayed indication that participants used CPS at work or that work outputs changed after the program.

"Organizational context" can include student participants if they are working on live sponsored business problems for an external organization, because the task setting is still organizationally anchored.
A useful review can mention applied outcomes, but its core claims should rest on studies that make at least some systematic attempt to assess impact rather than on anecdotal success stories.

members.name: Marcus Hale
members.expertise: Corporate training design, facilitation, innovation capability building, executive communication
members.background: Marcus leads enterprise-wide capability programs and has bought and adapted CPS-style workshops for product, operations, and HR teams; he is experienced in translating academic ideas into business-ready narratives for leaders.
members.private_state: He wants the brief to feel directly useful to senior leaders deciding whether to fund more creativity programs, and he needs examples that sound practical, varied, and close enough to what companies actually purchase.
hidden_assumptions: When people say CPS addresses "workplace issues," that includes realistic business cases, cross-functional challenge labs, and practice scenarios that mirror common work problems even if they are not a participant's own live issue.

"Effectiveness" mainly means that the training reliably produces better-quality ideas, stronger engagement, or implementable action plans within or immediately after the workshop, because that is the decision horizon leaders usually care about.
"Organizational context" means people employed inside companies or public organizations; student samples belong in the background at most, even if the students worked on company-sponsored projects.

If the brief is about balancing research and practice, it should treat documented client applications and internal post-program reports as meaningful evidence of value, even if they are not formal studies.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a workplace issue
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about focusing on CPS training for "workplace issues" or "real business challenges."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means actual, ongoing organizational problems tied to participants' work roles or a live client challenge with real consequences.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means any business-relevant challenge format, including simulated cases, challenge sprints, and generic operational scenarios that feel authentic to employees.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standard and shared in both academic and corporate settings, and both participants favor practical relevance, so neither expects the other to be using a narrower or broader meaning.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want to review the "effectiveness" of CPS training.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 takes effectiveness to require evidence that CPS changed behavior or outcomes beyond the session, such as later use on the job, implementation, or sustained performance effects.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 takes effectiveness to mean the training generated noticeably stronger ideas, clearer action plans, or positive manager reactions at the end of the workshop or shortly after.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both criteria sound reasonable and compatible in casual conversation, and brainstorming language around "impact" and "results" masks the fact that they are applying different thresholds of proof.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether student-on-company projects belong in scope
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to evidence from "organizational contexts" and examples involving "professionals or students on business challenges."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes these student-based projects can sit inside the main review if the challenge came from a real company and the task was genuinely organizational.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the main brief should center on employed workers, with student cases treated as peripheral or omitted because executives will not see them as workplace evidence.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The seed framing already pairs professionals and students together, so it feels like settled background context rather than a boundary that needs explicit negotiation.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to include application outcomes
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the brief should also include "outcomes of applying CPS to business challenges."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means extracting application outcomes from published or systematically documented sources and clearly separating them from training-effect evidence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means freely weaving in internal program summaries, client case snapshots, and facilitation debriefs as part of the practical evidence base.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because they are only brainstorming angles rather than discussing a formal review protocol, "include outcomes" sounds like a harmless framing choice rather than a methodological fork.

turns.inner_thought: I want this brief to be defensible if an academic colleague reads it. The key is to stay grounded in organizational settings and workplace issues, not drift into generic creativity rhetoric. And when we talk about whether CPS training is effective, I mean evidence that something changed after the session—use on the job, implementation, some downstream sign of transfer—not just that people enjoyed a workshop or produced ideas in the room.
turns.utterance: I think the brief should start from a very plain question: what do we really know about whether CPS training is effective in organizational settings? If we keep it anchored in workplace issues, rather than broad claims about creativity in general, it’ll be stronger for both the council and the conference audience.

turns.inner_thought: That framing works well for leaders as long as it feels practical. If we can show real business challenges and point to situations where CPS helped teams generate usable ideas fast, executives will lean in. For them, effectiveness is mostly about whether the workshop produces better outputs, momentum, and something they can act on right away.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. From the leadership side, it’ll land best if we can show real business challenges and make it concrete where CPS helped teams come up with usable ideas quickly. That makes the question of effectiveness feel immediately relevant.

turns.inner_thought: A sensible structure would separate studies where people are working on live organizational problems from evidence about what happens later. I also want room for sponsored project teams, including student teams on real company briefs, because some of those studies are better designed than the employee-only literature. If we keep the labels broad, Marcus will probably hear this as aligned.
turns.utterance: One way to structure it might be a section on studies where employees or sponsored project teams used CPS on workplace issues in organizational contexts, and then a second section on the evidence for effectiveness after the training. That would let us distinguish where the method has been used from what we know about what happens next.

turns.inner_thought: I should make sure we don't narrow the examples so much that the brief stops resembling what companies actually buy. Challenge labs, bootcamps, and business-case workshops are all recognizable to decision-makers and absolutely count as workplace-relevant to me, even if they aren't tied to someone's current role problem. I'll frame it broadly enough that Lena should still feel we're talking about practice.
turns.utterance: I like that. I’d also want us to cast the net wide enough to include things like challenge labs, internal innovation bootcamps, and business-case workshops, because from a buyer’s perspective those are still very much tied to workplace issues. If the brief reflects that range, it’ll feel closer to how organizations actually encounter CPS.

turns.inner_thought: This is where I should flag that some useful evidence comes from students on real company work. Those studies shouldn't be pushed to the margins if the business challenge is live and organizationally anchored. They may help the evidence base look less thin without relying on vendor-style anecdotes.
turns.utterance: And some of the stronger comparative papers actually involve students on business challenges tied to outside organizations. I’d be inclined to keep those in view as part of the evidence from organizational contexts, because they can round out the picture.

turns.inner_thought: Student material is fine as background, but if the main narrative leans on that, executives will tune out. They want to hear about employees inside firms dealing with business challenges that resemble their world. I can acknowledge the student cases without letting them define the brief.
turns.utterance: That makes sense as context. I’d just want the main story to feel unmistakably centered on employees dealing with workplace issues inside organizations, with the other material there to support rather than drive the narrative.

turns.inner_thought: Good, now I need to separate training effects from application outcomes. I don't want the brief to collapse workshop performance and actual workplace follow-through into one bucket. For me, effectiveness should not rest only on what happened during the session, and application outcomes should come from published or systematically documented sources, not just stories.
turns.utterance: Another distinction I’d really like us to preserve is between training effects and the outcomes of applying CPS to business challenges. That way, when we talk about effectiveness, we can show whether anything changed after the session rather than only what happened during it.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—that gives me space to bring in the practical material leaders care about. I can assemble internal summaries, client snapshots, and debrief notes showing action plans, follow-up moves, and implemented ideas. To me, those are exactly the kinds of application outcomes that make the case credible in business settings, even if they aren't formal studies.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. On that piece, I can pull together outcomes of applying CPS to business challenges from a range of prior programs—internal summaries, client stories, things that show action plans and implemented ideas. That would complement the research side nicely.

turns.inner_thought: If we anchor the brief around three questions, I can later sort the evidence more carefully without having that methodological debate now. The wording can stay broad: workplace issues, effectiveness, application cases. Marcus will hear something practical; I can still ensure the final claims are calibrated.
turns.utterance: So maybe the brief revolves around three framing questions: first, what workplace issues CPS training has been used on; second, what evidence exists for its effectiveness; and third, what the outcomes of applying CPS to business challenges suggest about business value. That feels like a clean way to organize the discussion.

turns.inner_thought: That gives me a very workable scaffold. I can populate each question with examples that feel concrete to leaders and still sound balanced enough for a conference proposal. As long as we blend research with practical cases, the innovation council will see both rigor and relevance.
turns.utterance: I’m on board with that. I’ll sketch some practical examples under each of those questions, and then we can shape it so the review feels balanced between research and practice for the innovation council.
